_comment: External tools, described by a command template and an output parser.
Each entry is disabled until you set "enabled": true and provide the paths it needs.
The command lines below are transcribed from each tool's published documentation and
have NOT been executed against the real software in this repository -- that is what
"verified": false means, and `python tools/run_tools.py check` prints it. Run once with
--dry-run to see the exact command that will be executed, and fix it here if the

tools.stands_for: published count-based segmentation; the closest prior art to ChromState's emission model
tools.how_to_enable: install EpiCSeg (Bioconductor/GitHub), then: export EPICSEG_R=/path/to/epicseg.R and set enabled=true
tools.notes: EpiCSeg's own counting step is bypassed so it sees ChromState's bins; check that its --counts reader accepts this matrix layout

tools.stands_for: the other widely used segmenter; continuous signal, no binarisation
tools.how_to_enable: install Segway + GMTK, build a genomedata archive from the exported counts, then: export SEGWAY_GENOMEDATA=/path/to/archive
tools.notes: two-step tool: `segway train` then `segway identify` writes the BED. Extend this entry or run identify yourself before parsing

tools.stands_for: continuous chromatin state features; direct prior art for quantitative state scores
tools.how_to_enable: install epigenome-ssm, then: export EPIGENOME_SSM_CMD='python -m epigenome_ssm' (or the installed entry point)
tools.notes: emits continuous features, not labels; you need an argmax/threshold step to produce labels.txt, or compare its features directly

tools.stands_for: count-based segmentation with per-mark distribution choice and explicit duration modelling; the closest published competitor to ChromState's emission model
tools.how_to_enable: install EpiSegMix from its repository, write a thin wrapper that accepts the flags above (or edit them to match the installed CLI), then: export EPISEGMIX_CMD=/path/to/wrapper
tools.notes: EpiSegMix selects a distribution per mark (Poisson, NB, zero-inflated, ...) and models segment length explicitly. Record which distributions it picked; ChromState's `zinb` emission is the comparable in-process row

tools.stands_for: two-level annotation: bin-level states nested in domain-level states (Marco et al., Nat Commun 2017)
tools.how_to_enable: install diHMM (MATLAB or its Python port), export DIHMM_CMD, set DIHMM_BINARY_DIR to the folder written by `chromstate export-chromhmm`, and DIHMM_DOMAIN_STATES (e.g. 30)
tools.notes: diHMM consumes ChromHMM-style binarised input, so it inherits binarisation; the bin-level BED is what is scored here. The domain-level BED is a separate output and has no counterpart in a flat segmenter

tools.stands_for: per-mark enrichment caller (binomial mixture of ChIP vs control), not a joint segmenter; commonly used to define bivalent regions
tools.how_to_enable: install Bioconductor normR, write an R script that runs enrichR/regimeR per mark on the exported counts (needs a control column) and writes one combinatorial-state label per bin, then: export NORMR_R=/path/to/script.R
tools.notes: normR needs a control track; the exported count matrix must include the control columns. Its output is per-mark enrichment, so combining marks into `n_states` labels is a step the wrapper must define (the in-process normr_like row uses k-means on enrichment probabilities)
